blocks.content: kubectl cordon marks a node as unschedulable, without touching any Pods already running there, a much gentler action than drain, covered in the previous topic.
cordon flags a node so the scheduler, covered in the Architecture module, will no longer consider it a candidate for new Pods, existing behavior on the node is otherwise completely unaffected.

blocks.alt: A flag for the scheduler, nothing more, existing behavior untouched

blocks.content: This is the genuinely important contrast with drain, cordoning a node does not evict anything already running there, those Pods keep running exactly as they were, cordon only affects future scheduling decisions.

blocks.alt: Nothing already there is evicted, only future scheduling decisions are affected

blocks.content: 3. New Pods Simply Won't Land There
blocks.text: 3. New Pods Simply Won't Land There

blocks.content: Any new Pod the scheduler needs to place will now skip this node entirely, regardless of how much free capacity it actually has, it is treated as ineligible for the duration of the cordon.

blocks.alt: Treated as ineligible for new placements, however much free capacity it actually has

blocks.content: Cordoning a node is a common, gentler preparation step, either standalone (when you want to stop new work landing there but are not ready to evict what is already running) or as part of the full drain process covered in the previous topic.

blocks.alt: A gentler preparation step, either standalone or as part of a full drain

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: kubectl cordon marks a node unschedulable for new Pods, without evicting anything already running there, a much gentler action than drain.
It is a common preparation step, either standalone, or as the automatic first part of the full drain process covered in the previous topic.
